input: What does reciprocal rank fusion combine?
expected: It combines ranked lists from multiple retrievers by summing reciprocal rank scores.
contexts: Reciprocal rank fusion merges ranked lists from multiple retrievers by summing 1/(k + rank) scores.

input: Why does BLEU apply a brevity penalty?
expected: To stop short outputs from inflating precision.
contexts: BLEU applies a brevity penalty so that very short candidates cannot achieve high precision with few n-grams.

input: What is the difference between Recall@k and MRR?
expected: Recall@k measures how many relevant items appear in the top k, while MRR rewards the rank of the first relevant item.
contexts: Recall@k counts relevant items in the top k. MRR is the reciprocal rank of the first relevant result.

expected: It discounts relevant results that appear lower in the ranked list.
contexts: nDCG discounts each relevant result by a logarithmic function of its rank.

input: Why add overlap between adjacent chunks?
expected: Overlap preserves facts that would otherwise be split across chunk boundaries.
contexts: Adjacent chunk overlap keeps sentences and facts intact when a document is divided into fixed-size windows.

input: What is a known limitation of exact match?
expected: It gives no credit to semantically correct paraphrases.
contexts: Exact match compares normalised strings, so a correct paraphrase scores zero.

input: Why should an LLM judge be calibrated against humans?
expected: Because model judgments can drift and disagree with human raters.
contexts: Judge scores drift across model versions, so calibration against a human-labelled set is required before gating releases.

expected: The latency below which 95 percent of requests fall.
contexts: The p95 latency is the value below which 95 percent of observed request latencies fall.

input: How does a relative tolerance differ from an absolute tolerance?
expected: A relative tolerance scales with the baseline value, while an absolute tolerance is a fixed score margin.
contexts: Absolute tolerance is a fixed margin. Relative tolerance is a fraction of the baseline, so it scales with the metric.

input: What is the purpose of a held-out evaluation split?
expected: To estimate performance on data that was not used to tune the system.
contexts: A held-out split estimates generalisation on examples excluded from prompt and retrieval tuning.
